planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay above 55°F. Give plants full sun and steady moisture through fruit set for the heaviest yields.

directions: Georgia Flame is an old heirloom pepper from the country of Georgia in the Caucasus, not the American state, passed down as a dual-purpose sweet-to-mild roasting pepper for generations there. Plants set an abundance of long, tapered, conical pods that ripen from green to a deep, glossy red, with thick walls and a fruity flavor that sits right at the sweet-hot border, roughly on par with a mild jalapeno. Because the pods hold their shape and thick flesh under high heat, they are especially well suited to open-flame roasting, grilling, and salsa, and the plants are vigorous, heavy producers once established in warm soil.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; the compact 18-inch plants do well in containers or raised beds and need no staking.

directions: Pimento L is a compact, open-pollinated pimiento-type sweet pepper long grown in home gardens for its heart-shaped, thick-walled fruit and reliable tobacco mosaic virus resistance, a trait that made it a dependable choice before modern hybrid pimientos were widely available. Fruits run about four and a half inches long, ripening from green to a glossy bright red with very few seeds and exceptionally sweet, mild flesh (under 500 Scoville units). The short, tidy plants make this a good fit for small beds or containers, and the thick walls hold up well for stuffing, roasting, or slicing raw into salads.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once all frost danger has passed and give plants consistent moisture through fruiting.

directions: NuMex Joe E. Parker was released in 1990 by New Mexico State University's chile breeding program and named for a longtime agricultural evaluator who helped select it; it is one of the standard named cultivars behind commercial Hatch green chile alongside NuMex Big Jim. Pods run six to eight inches, thick-walled and mild to medium in heat, and are traditionally picked green for roasting and stuffing or left to ripen red for drying and sauces. The plants are productive and relatively compact for a New Mexico-type chile, making them a manageable choice for home gardeners who want authentic Hatch flavor without the largest-fruited varieties.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; stake or cage this indeterminate vine, and expect steady production right up to frost.

directions: Mule Team belongs to a small family of Americana-named heirloom tomatoes developed by the same hobbyist breeder as Box Car Willie, and the seed nearly disappeared before being rediscovered stored in glass jars decades later and grown out by tomato collector Dr. Carolyn Male. The sturdy, drought-tolerant indeterminate vines are abundant producers of eight to twelve ounce beefsteak fruit with rich, juicy, zippy-sweet flavor, and the plants keep fruit quality consistent from the first harvest through the last frost of the season rather than tapering off in late summer heat. It is a dependable choice for gardeners who want a hearty slicing tomato without the fussiness of some other large-fruited heirlooms.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; half-runners send out short runners so a light trellis or brush support improves yield and airflow.

directions: Non-Tough Half Runner is a preserved Appalachian bean selected and maintained by Dr. Bill Best of the Sustainable Mountain Agriculture Center after decades of commercial half-runner seed losing the tenderness that once made the type popular, as seed producers had inadvertently bred in a toughening trait to extend shelf life. Its plump pods stay tender-eating even when the seeds inside swell to full size, which sets it apart from most modern half-runners that toughen quickly, and it remains a favorite for traditional leather-britches drying as well as fresh snap use, canning, and freezing. The half-runner growth habit sends out short runners beyond a bush frame, so light support or brush keeps pods off the ground and easy to pick.

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed at the base of a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis; vigorous vines need real climbing support and will keep producing if kept picked.

directions: Tar Heel is an old pole bean reportedly carried west by North Carolina natives from the Jackson/Haywood county area who migrated to Washington state for timber work around the turn of the twentieth century, taking on the Tar Heel name in honor of that origin. The vigorous climbing vines are heavy yielders of five to six inch, flattened pods that bulge as the seeds inside develop, with a hearty, old-fashioned flavor reminiscent of a greasy bean even though the pod surface itself is not shiny. It is a good pick for gardeners who want a traditional pole snap bean with real heirloom character rather than a modern high-production hybrid.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm and frost risk has passed; train the vigorous climbing vines onto a sturdy trellis to keep the long fruit straight and off the ground.

directions: Trombetta di Albenga is a climbing zucchetta-type summer squash from the Ligurian coast of Italy, related to the more widely known Tromboncino but grown and selected as its own distinct regional strain around the town of Albenga. The curved, trumpet-shaped fruit reaches twelve to fifteen inches and is prized for its firm, nearly seedless flesh concentrated in the long neck (seeds sit only in the small bulbous end), with a mild, artichoke-like flavor that holds up better than typical zucchini when sliced and sauteed. Because it is a true climber, giving it a trellis rather than letting it sprawl saves garden space and produces straighter, easier-to-harvest fruit; left on the vine past the summer-squash stage it also matures into a nutty-flavored winter squash.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows for good pollination. This variety was bred for cool Pacific Northwest summers, so in zone 9a it performs best sown as early as soil temperature allows to mature before peak summer heat.

directions: Hooker's Sweet Indian was developed more than seventy years ago by Ira Hooker near Olympia, Washington, who worked from Native American corn strains to produce a sweet corn that would reliably ripen in a short, cool growing season. The short four to four-and-a-half foot stalks are unusually compact for a corn variety and typically set two ears per plant, five to seven inches long with 10-12 rows of kernels, starting out white and darkening through purple to a deep blue-black as they dry. Because it holds sweetness at the fresh eating stage and also grinds into flavorful cornmeal once fully dried, it works as a genuine dual-purpose corn for gardeners who want both a fresh crop and a grain harvest from the same planting.
